rationale: A wins because it prunes harder and keeps the angles cleaner: “The hard part of a circular sneaker is the mail” is a real operations story, not launch confetti. B has the best single accountability headline, “On says its shoe subscription ‘closes the loop’ — it won’t say how big the loop is,” but then dilutes itself with “does the rest of the running category have to follow?” That is the kind of question that sounds smart until an editor asks, based on what?
gaps_in_A: “moving a core product from purchase to subscription nationwide” overstates the fact pattern; the update supports one Cyclon subscription going nationwide, not a core product line moving from sales to subscription.
“commercial-scale test” and “pilot volume to nationwide distribution” are a little too grand. Nationwide availability is not the same as proven commercial scale or volume.
“take-back programs are widely seen as the operational graveyard of circular retail” may be true, but it is not grounded in the supplied update. Bring evidence or turn it into a question.
It misses a clean standalone accountability angle around “close the loop” versus undisclosed recycling rate; that is sitting right there with a knife and fork.
gaps_in_B: “does a nationwide rollout prove shoppers will accept access-not-ownership” overclaims. A rollout proves On is trying it nationally; acceptance needs subscriber, retention, or renewal data.

“On bets runners will pay monthly to never own their shoes” and “Shoes join the rental economy” are too close. One is the access-over-ownership story; the other is the same story wearing a different jacket.

“does the rest of the running category have to follow?” is speculative without competitor programs, analyst context, or market-share pressure in the update. It is a trade follow-up, not a primary angle yet.
“servicization” is consultant fog. A reporter can understand subscription shoes without being dragged through a white paper.
